surfaces.part: left window/awning wall section (blue panes, brown bars)
central dark navy panel with cream pillar strip

answer.evidence: The cell is a 13x15 fragment of a larger kit. Every part is drawn as a vertical face: blue window panes, brown wood, a dark navy panel, a cream strip and a brown post. The silhouette is a constant 13 px wide on rows 0-14, so there is no ellipse or widening. The column scans show no front-edge line or eave shadow at any top band, and no roof, awning or lintel slope is visible. The cream band at rows 10-12 and the grey row 13 form a base or threshold strip of 1-3 rows, not a top surface. The whole cell is a flat front elevation with no horizontal top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny sprite of about 12x14 source pixels, smaller than one 16x16 tile. It looks like a small icon or prop with a blue and white panel, a brown post and an orange accent. It has no roof, no wall mass and no door or windows, so it is not a whole building like the references. The measured facts (17 visible tones, 0% near-flat, 0% neutral dark edges) are favourable. But they come from a few dense, busy pixels, not from material ramps. The references show 5-6 step tile-roof ramps with per-tile highlights, plaster speckle and stone shaded one by one, and the candidate shows nothing comparable. I count only about 3 lightness steps on any single material. The outline is dark and loosely tinted but not applied consistently. Since the piece cannot be compared fairly with building-scale references and is clearly thinner and simpler than them, it fails.

answer.evidence: The tile is a 13x15 fragment of a wall seen face-on. Rows 0-9 are vertical faces: a blue window with a wood frame, a dark navy panel and an orange-brown vertical strip. Rows 10-12 are a beige band, and row 13 is a grey edge line over a dark row 14. This could be a floor or sill strip, but it is only 3 rows with no ellipse, no roof or awning plane, and no eave shadow, so I read it as a base band rather than a top surface. The width is a constant 13 for all 15 rows, so nothing narrows or widens to suggest a roof, lid or cap. The piece has no top slope or roof, so it reads as a front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a tiny icon-sized object, about one tile or less. It has no readable roof, walls or door, so it is not a whole building like the two references. The references are large, with per-tile roof scallops, timber framing and stone shaded stone by stone. The facts point the same way. The candidate has 17 distinct colours in total, against 185 and 66 for the references, and its 17 tones per tile come from a very small, cramped area. Its dark edge pixels are tinted (0% neutral), so the outline is not a near-black sticker line, and it has no flat 5x5 fills. But it has only about 3 shading steps per material and no roof-tile or stone texture, so it falls well short of the Beodeul building standard in structure and richness. The kind mismatch alone is enough to fail it.
